# COMP 351 — Ethics in Computing and Information Systems
## Master Compilation — Reflection Log (🧭) & Activities

This master document combines all 24 Reflection Log items and all 20 Action/Activity items into a single file, arranged in **course-progression order** (Part → Unit → Section). Within each section, activities (videos, readings, quizzes, submissions) and reflections are interleaved in the order they occur in the course, so the document reads as a continuous record of the course from orientation through the final portfolio.

- **Reflections (R01–R24)** are the graded/posted 🧭 Reflection Log entries — each contains the original task prompt and the student's written reflection.
- **Actions (A01–A20)** are the supporting quizzes, videos, podcasts, readings, and assignment submissions — each contains the task and a summary with references.

### R01 — Course Intentions & Study Schedule

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (1 of 24) · **Section:** 1.1 Making a Successful Start · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Build your study schedule using the sample schedule in the Course Orientation; mark intended start/completion dates for each unit and activity within your contract dates.

Post your introduction AND a copy of your study schedule in your Reflection Log.

*Note: You cannot proceed to Unit 2 until you pass the Plagiarism Awareness Quiz (100% required, multiple attempts allowed).*

#### My Reflection

**Introduction**

Hello everyone. My name is Nguyen and I am taking COMP351 because I work with computers and data every day, but I have never stopped to think carefully about the ethics behind what I build and use. What I hope to learn is how to recognize ethical problems before they become real harms, and how to make defensible decisions when there is no obvious right answer.

A good example of data I use is the personal contact and account information I handle at work. I use it to set up user accounts, troubleshoot login problems, and send notifications. The systems cannot function without knowing who the user is, but handling it has made me realize how much trust people place in me when they hand over their details. At home, I use data like my own banking and fitness-app information to track spending and exercise, which made me notice how often I accept terms without really reading them.

I am looking forward to the discussions on privacy, algorithms, and AI, because those topics touch both my job and my daily life.

**Study Schedule**

Working within my contract dates, I have mapped out the four parts of the course so I finish with time to spare for the assignments.

### A01 — Academic Integrity & Plagiarism Awareness Quiz

- **Type:** Action (1 of 20) · **Section:** 1.1 Making a Successful Start · **Status:** Done
- **MANDATORY GATE:** You cannot proceed to Unit 2 until you pass (100% required; multiple attempts allowed).

#### Task

Review the Student Academic Code of Conduct (AU's academic integrity policy).
Read the Write Site resources: 'The Basics of Documentation' and 'Avoiding Plagiarism'.
Take the mandatory Plagiarism Awareness Quiz.

#### Summary & Notes

This action is a course requirement, not a media review. It asks you to study Athabasca University's Student Academic Code of Conduct, read the Write Site guides "The Basics of Documentation" and "Avoiding Plagiarism," and then pass the mandatory Plagiarism Awareness Quiz. Academic integrity policies explain what counts as cheating, plagiarism, and improper collaboration, and they spell out the penalties for breaking the rules. The Write Site documentation resources teach you how to cite sources correctly, when to quote versus paraphrase, and how to keep track of where ideas come from so you never accidentally pass off someone else's work as your own. The quiz checks that you understand these ideas before you start writing graded assignments.

Key takeaways: plagiarism includes copying text, using ideas without credit, and even reusing your own past work without saying so (self-plagiarism). Proper documentation (APA style in this course) protects you and gives credit to original authors. The quiz allows multiple attempts but requires a perfect score to continue.

Why this matters for ethics in computing: honesty about sources is a core professional value. Engineers and computer scientists who misrepresent data, code, or research damage trust and can cause real harm. Building good citation habits now supports ethical practice later.

**⚠️ Student action required:** Read the AU Academic Code of Conduct and the two Write Site guides, then complete the mandatory Plagiarism Awareness Quiz in the course LMS and score 100% (multiple attempts allowed). You cannot proceed to Unit 2 until you pass.

**References**

Athabasca University. (n.d.). *Student academic misconduct policy*. https://www.athabascau.ca/university-secretariat/_documents/policy/student-academic-misconduct-policy.pdf

Athabasca University Write Site. (n.d.). *Avoiding plagiarism*. Athabasca University. https://www.athabascau.ca/write-site/

## Unit 2 — Ethical Orientation

### A02 — Philosopher Personality Test & Moral Machine

- **Type:** Action (2 of 20) · **Section:** 2.1 Why Bother with Ethics and Philosophy? · **Status:** Done
- *Supports Reflection R02 (Personal Philosophy).*

#### Task

Take the Philosopher Personality Test to assess which philosopher you most align with.
Try the self-driving car moral dilemmas on MIT's Moral Machine.

#### Summary & Notes

This action has two interactive parts. First, take a Philosopher Personality Test, which asks a series of questions about your beliefs and then matches you to historical thinkers such as Socrates, Kant, Nietzsche, Aristotle, or Confucius. The best-known version is the IDRlabs test, which scores you against seven philosophers. The result is meant to start self-reflection, not to be a scientific label, and you may match different philosophers in different parts of your life. Second, try MIT's Moral Machine, an online tool that puts you in the seat of a self-driving car facing "trolley problem" dilemmas: should the car swerve or stay, save passengers or pedestrians, spare the young or the old? The Moral Machine collected about 40 million decisions from people in 233 countries. Researchers found that moral choices are not universal; preferences cluster into three groups of countries shaped by culture and institutions.

Key takeaways: ethics is not one fixed set of answers, and reasonable people disagree. Machines that make life-or-death choices force programmers to turn fuzzy human values into hard rules.

Why this matters for ethics in computing: self-driving cars and other automated systems must encode moral choices in code. Understanding your own ethical leanings, and how they differ across cultures, helps designers build systems that are fair and accountable.

**⚠️ Student action required:** Complete the Philosopher Personality Test and run through several Moral Machine scenarios yourself, then record your reactions in Reflection R02 (Personal Philosophy).

**References**

IDRlabs. (n.d.). *Philosopher personality test*. https://www.idrlabs.com/philosopher-personality/test.php

Awad, E., Dsouza, S., Kim, R., Schulz, J., Henrich, J., Shariff, A., Bonnefon, J.-F., & Rahwan, I. (2018). The moral machine experiment. *Nature, 563*, 59–64. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-018-0637-6

Massachusetts Institute of Technology Media Lab. (n.d.). *Moral machine*. https://www.moralmachine.net/

### R02 — Personal Philosophy Reflection

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (2 of 24) · **Section:** 2.1 Why Bother with Ethics and Philosophy? · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Post a reflection titled "Personal Philosophy Reflection" that includes:
- a statement of an ethical action you have previously taken.
- a philosophy or belief that may have (in hindsight) informed your perspective in that action.
- a comment on the impact of the ethical action on you now.
- an answer to: Will you behave differently going forward?

*Prep: Take the Philosopher Personality Test and try MIT's Moral Machine. Required reading: Quinn, Ch. 2 'Introduction to Ethics'.*

#### My Reflection

An ethical action I took was at a previous job, when I found that a shared spreadsheet held customer phone numbers that the whole team could open, even people who had no reason to see them. I could have ignored it because it was not my project, but I flagged it to my manager and suggested we lock the file down. It created some awkwardness with the colleague who built the sheet, but the access was restricted within a week.

Looking back, I think a duty-based belief informed me. I felt people had a right to have their information protected, regardless of whether anyone had actually been harmed yet. That lines up with what Quinn (2020) calls deontological thinking, where an action is judged by the duty behind it rather than only by the result. Trying MIT's Moral Machine made me realize how much harder ethics gets when every choice hurts someone, and how my "rights" instinct does not always give a clean answer. The Moral Machine study found people generally wanted to spare more lives and younger lives, but those preferences varied a lot by culture (Awad et al., 2018).

The impact on me now is that I trust my instinct to speak up, even when it is inconvenient. Going forward I will behave a little differently. Instead of waiting until I stumble on a problem, I want to ask about data access and privacy at the start of a project, so issues are prevented rather than caught late.

**References**

Awad, E., Dsouza, S., Kim, R., Schulz, J., Henrich, J., Shariff, A., Bonnefon, J.-F., & Rahwan, I. (2018). The Moral Machine experiment. *Nature, 563*(7729), 59–64. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-018-0637-6

Quinn, M. J. (2020). *Ethics for the information age* (8th ed.). Pearson.

### R03 — Does My Ethical Position Change with Context?

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (3 of 24) · **Section:** 2.1 Why Bother with Ethics and Philosophy? · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Post a reflection titled "Does My Ethical Position Change with Context?" that includes:
- an answer to: How do Barger's ethical stances fit with your own perspectives?
- a comment considering each of the three dilemmas Barger presents (piracy, privacy, and power/authority).

*Required reading: Robert Barger, Ch. 6 'Can We Find a Single Ethical Code?' in Ermann & Shauf (eds.), Computers, Ethics, and Society.*

#### My Reflection

Barger argues that even though people hold many different ethical theories, we may still be able to find shared ground when we reason carefully about real cases (Barger, 2003). That fits my own perspective fairly well. I do not think there is one single code that answers every question, but I do believe most reasonable people can agree on basic ideas like "do not cause needless harm" and "be honest." So I sit somewhere in the middle: I am open to different frameworks, but I look for the common core they share.

Thinking through Barger's three dilemmas helped me test that. On **piracy**, my first reaction is that copying software or media without paying is wrong because it takes someone's work, but I notice my position softens when the price is unfair or the product is no longer sold. That tells me my stance is not purely rule-based. On **privacy**, I feel strongly that people should control their own information, and here my position barely changes with context, which surprised me. On **power and authority**, I am most conflicted. I usually respect rules and the people who set them, but Barger's point pushed me to admit that authority can be wrong, and that blindly obeying is not the same as acting ethically.

So does my position change with context? Partly. My privacy stance is stable, but my views on piracy and authority clearly shift depending on the situation, which shows I lean more on consequences than I first assumed.

**References**

Barger, R. N. (2003). Can we find a single ethical code? In M. D. Ermann & M. S. Shauf (Eds.), *Computers, ethics, and society* (3rd ed., pp. 42–47). Oxford University Press.

## Unit 3 — Critical and Logical Skill Assessment

### A03 — Logic Skills: Notation & Khan Academy

- **Type:** Action (3 of 20) · **Section:** 3.1 Logical Skills · **Status:** Done

#### Task

Review Commonly Used Mathematical Notation (for use in logic).
Complete Khan Academy Logic Toolbox exercises:
- Conditional Reasoning and Logical Equivalence
- If X, then Y | Sufficiency and Necessity
- The Logic of 'If' vs. 'Only if'
- A Quick Guide to Translating Common Prose Statements into Conditional Logic Statements

#### Summary & Notes

This action builds the formal-logic skills you need to analyze ethical arguments later in the course. You first review common mathematical and logical notation (symbols for "and," "or," "not," "if...then," "if and only if," and quantifiers). Then you complete Khan Academy's Logic Toolbox exercises, which focus on conditional reasoning. The exercises cover: conditional statements and logical equivalence; the structure "if X, then Y" and the difference between a sufficient condition and a necessary condition; the contrast between "if" and "only if"; and how to translate everyday prose sentences into precise conditional logic statements.

Key takeaways: a conditional "if P then Q" means P is sufficient for Q, and Q is necessary for P. "P only if Q" actually means "if P then Q," which trips many people up. A statement and its contrapositive ("if not Q then not P") are logically equivalent, while the converse and inverse are not. Translating plain English into logic carefully prevents reasoning errors.

Why this matters for ethics in computing: clear logical thinking lets you test whether an ethical or technical argument is valid, spot hidden assumptions, and avoid fallacies. The same skills underpin writing correct code, designing algorithms, and evaluating claims about technology.

**⚠️ Student action required:** Work through the Khan Academy Logic Toolbox exercises listed in the task yourself; the practice is interactive and is not something that can be completed on your behalf.

**References**

Khan Academy. (n.d.). *Logic toolbox*. https://www.khanacademy.org/

Klement, K. C. (n.d.). *Propositional logic*. Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. https://iep.utm.edu/prop-log/

### R04 — Rules in Canada

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (4 of 24) · **Section:** 3.2 Rules · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Conduct an internet search for an example of a rule, common law, and/or policy involving CS or IS in a country where you work or are likely to work.
Post a reflection titled "Rules in <your country of choice>" that includes:
- a statement describing, with links, a rule or policy you found.
- a comment on its impact on you.
- how you will behave differently now that you have this knowledge.

#### My Reflection

**Rules in Canada**

The rule I found is Canada's *Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act* (PIPEDA), the federal privacy law that governs how private-sector organizations collect, use, and disclose personal information in commercial activities (Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, n.d.). It is built on ten fair information principles, including consent, limiting collection, safeguards, and accountability, and it requires organizations to report breaches that pose a real risk of significant harm. The official summary is here: https://www.priv.gc.ca/en/privacy-topics/privacy-laws-in-canada/the-personal-information-protection-and-electronic-documents-act-pipeda/pipeda_brief/

The impact on me is fairly direct. Canada is where I work, and PIPEDA means that any system I help build or operate that touches customer data has legal duties attached to it. The principle that stood out most is "limiting collection," which says you should only gather the data you actually need. In the past I assumed more data was always better for future features, so this changed how I think.

How I will behave differently: I will start treating data minimization as a default. Before adding a field to a form or logging a new value, I will ask whether we genuinely need it and whether we have meaningful consent to collect it. I will also pay closer attention to how long we keep data, since PIPEDA expects information to be destroyed when it is no longer needed rather than kept indefinitely.

**References**

Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada. (n.d.). *PIPEDA in brief*. https://www.priv.gc.ca/en/privacy-topics/privacy-laws-in-canada/the-personal-information-protection-and-electronic-documents-act-pipeda/pipeda_brief/

### R05 — My Critical Thinking

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (5 of 24) · **Section:** 3.3 Critical Thinking Skills · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Watch the Critical Thinking Skills video (University of London) from 22:00 to 30:00.
Post a reflection titled "My Critical Thinking" that includes:
- a statement describing one take-away from the critical thinking model.
- a comment on its expected impact on you.
- an answer to: Which critical thinking skill would you build or enhance in yourself, and how will you incorporate it into your working or studying life?

#### My Reflection

My main take-away from the critical thinking model is that good thinking moves through stages rather than jumping straight to a verdict. A common version of the model starts with **description** (asking what, where, who, and why to set the context), moves to **analysis** (asking how and what if to break the topic apart), and ends with **evaluation** (asking "so what?" and "what next?" to judge significance and decide what to do). What struck me is that the model is not meant to be strictly linear; you move back and forth between the stages (University of Leeds, n.d.).

The expected impact on me is that I will slow down before reacting. I tend to read something and immediately decide if I agree, which means I skip the description and analysis stages and go straight to evaluation. Naming the stages gives me a checklist to catch that habit.

The skill I most want to build is the analysis stage, specifically asking "what if" and questioning assumptions before I judge. In my working life, I plan to apply it in code reviews and design discussions by deliberately asking "what assumption is this built on?" before I support or reject an idea. In my studying life, I will use the same questions on readings, writing a short description-analysis-evaluation note for key sources instead of just highlighting them. That should make my reflections deeper and my decisions at work better reasoned.

**References**

University of Leeds. (n.d.). *A model for critical thinking*. Leeds University Library. https://library.leeds.ac.uk/info/1401/academic-skills/105/critical-thinking/2

### R06 — Update: Does My Ethical Position Change with Context?

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (6 of 24) · **Section:** 3.4 Considering Ethics in CS and IS · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Revisit your earlier post "Does My Ethical Position Change with Context?"
Post a reflection titled "Update – Does my Ethical Position Change with Context?" that includes:
- Have your perspectives changed after completing Unit 3?
- Are there any parts of the ethical frameworks you are unlikely to apply to your thinking? Why?

*Required reading: Spinello, Ch. 2 'Frameworks for Ethical Analysis'; review Quinn, Ch. 2 if needed.*

#### My Reflection

Going back to my earlier post, my perspectives have changed in one important way after Unit 3. Before, I described myself as someone who looks for the "common core" across ethical theories. After reading Spinello's frameworks, I now have clearer names for what I was doing. Spinello distinguishes teleological theories like utilitarianism, which judge actions by their consequences, from deontological theories, which judge actions by duty regardless of the outcome, and he also gives weight to natural rights such as privacy and bodily integrity (Spinello, 2014). Having those categories made me realize my privacy stance is really a rights-based position, while my flexible views on piracy were consequence-based. So my views did not flip, but I understand them better and can defend them more clearly.

Are there parts of these frameworks I am unlikely to apply? Yes. I am unlikely to apply strict act-by-act utilitarianism, where every single choice is recalculated for the greatest good. In real situations I cannot reliably predict or measure all the consequences, and it can be used to justify harming a few people for the benefit of many, which I am uncomfortable with. I am also cautious about rigid deontology that never bends, because real cases sometimes have duties that conflict. I expect to keep using a mix: rights and duties as my baseline, with a consequences check on top.

**References**

Spinello, R. A. (2014). *Cyberethics: Morality and law in cyberspace* (5th ed.). Jones & Bartlett Learning.

### R07 — Ranking Five Ethical Positions

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (7 of 24) · **Section:** 3.4 Considering Ethics in CS and IS · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Post a reflection ranking the following five ethical positions (1 = most likely, 5 = least likely):
- My actions follow longstanding accepted rules. I avoid logical contradictions.
- My actions are ethical because they are consistent with the actions of a virtuous person.
- My actions can break a rule when my society would benefit from it and rational people would accept my actions.
- My actions are ethical if each action results in a net good, even if some results are not desirable or some rules are broken.
- My actions follow rules that—if everyone followed them—would bring about the greatest good in the long term.

*Also (Action): Note at least three of the most interesting computing-in-society stories for use-case selection. Take the mandatory Ethical Thinking Quiz (100% to proceed).*

#### My Reflection

Here is my ranking, from most likely (1) to least likely (5) to describe how I actually act. I have named the theory each statement matches so my reasoning is clear (Quinn, 2020).

1. **"My actions follow rules that, if everyone followed them, would bring about the greatest good in the long term."** (Rule utilitarianism.) This is closest to how I think. It keeps the stability of rules but ties them to good outcomes over time, which feels both practical and principled.

2. **"My actions can break a rule when society would benefit and rational people would accept it."** (Social contract reasoning.) I ranked this second because I do believe rules can be broken when there is a fair, agreed reason, but I am cautious about how easily this can be abused.

3. **"My actions are ethical because they are consistent with a virtuous person."** (Virtue ethics.) I admire this and often ask "what would a good person do?", but it is vague as a decision rule, so it guides me more than it decides for me.

4. **"My actions follow longstanding accepted rules and avoid logical contradictions."** (Kantian/rule deontology.) I respect duties, but ranking it fourth because I will not follow a rule just because it is old or accepted if it produces clear harm.

5. **"My actions are ethical if each results in a net good, even if some results are undesirable or rules are broken."** (Act utilitarianism.) Least likely, because recalculating every single action invites rationalizing harm to a few for the many.

**Three computing-in-society stories I noted for use cases:** (1) facial recognition and wrongful arrests, (2) the right-to-repair fight over John Deere tractors, and (3) algorithmic teacher-evaluation systems. Each raises strong ethical questions I want to explore further.

**References**

Quinn, M. J. (2020). *Ethics for the information age* (8th ed.). Pearson.

# Part 2: About the Data

## Unit 4 — What is Data, Really?

### R08 — IoT Stories Analysis

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (8 of 24) · **Section:** 4.3 Why Big Data Became a Game Changer · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Review media websites for stories about the IoT in the last five years. Select two to add to your Reflection Log.
For each case, identify:
- what data would be needed for the device to operate successfully.
- how users communicate with the device.
- whether privacy issues may arise.
- what physical controls, if any, are evident.

*Required reading: RSS/IFoA Guide for Ethical Data Science (includes a useful implementation checklist).*

#### My Reflection

I picked two IoT stories from the last few years and analyzed each one.

**Case 1 — Amazon Ring smart doorbells.** In 2023 the FTC settled with Ring for $5.8 million after finding that employees and contractors had been able to view customers' private videos, including footage from bedrooms and bathrooms, and that Ring had shared footage with police (Federal Trade Commission, 2023).
- *Data needed:* live and recorded video, motion-sensor triggers, timestamps, the home's location, and the owner's account details.
- *How users communicate with it:* a smartphone app and voice or chime alerts; users tap to view clips, talk through the speaker, and manage sharing.
- *Privacy issues:* clearly yes. The device records visitors and neighbours who never consented, and the footage can be accessed by staff or handed to police, sometimes without the owner's permission.
- *Physical controls:* the camera can be physically unplugged or angled away, and there is a hardware on/off for some models, but once data is in the cloud the owner has little physical control.

**Case 2 — Smart thermostats (e.g., Nest).** These learn a household's routine to save energy.
- *Data needed:* indoor temperature, motion/occupancy, schedules, and sometimes location to know when you are home.
- *How users communicate with it:* an app, a wall dial, and voice assistants.
- *Privacy issues:* occupancy data reveals when a home is empty, which is sensitive if leaked or sold.
- *Physical controls:* a manual dial and the ability to disable motion sensing give the user more direct control than the doorbell does.

Both cases show the pattern the RSS/IFoA guide warns about: devices quietly collect more than users expect, so privacy should be designed in from the start (Royal Statistical Society & Institute and Faculty of Actuaries, 2019).

**References**

Federal Trade Commission. (2023, May 31). *Ring's privacy failures led to spying and harassment through home security cameras*. https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2023/05/rings-privacy-failures-led-spying-harassment-through-home-security-cameras

Royal Statistical Society & Institute and Faculty of Actuaries. (2019). *A guide for ethical data science*. https://rss.org.uk/

### A05 — TED Talks: Meaning, Books & Data Presentation

- **Type:** Action (5 of 20) · **Section:** 4.5 Data Misuse · **Status:** Done

#### Task

Watch Susan Etlinger's TED Talk on big data (meaning comes from humans, not data).
Watch Erez Lieberman Aiden & Jean-Baptiste Michel's TED Talk about 5 million books (don't mistake correlation for causation).
Watch Mona Chalabi's TED Talk on interpreting data and how presentation affects meaning.

#### Summary & Notes

This action pairs three TED Talks that all warn against trusting data blindly. Susan Etlinger's "What do we do with all this big data?" argues that data does not create meaning, people do. As we collect more data, we need stronger critical-thinking skills drawn from the humanities, ethics, and social science. She shows how a project with the CDC had to understand how people actually talk about smoking and e-cigarettes before the numbers made sense, and she warns that data which simply makes you feel comfortable is probably being read wrong. Erez Lieberman Aiden and Jean-Baptiste Michel's "What we learned from 5 million books" introduces the Google Ngram Viewer and "culturomics," using 500 billion words to track cultural change. Their fun results come with a caution: patterns in data show correlation, not proof of cause. Mona Chalabi's "3 ways to spot a bad statistic" gives practical tests: can you see the uncertainty, how was the data gathered, and who had an incentive to shape it? She insists anyone can learn to question numbers.

Key takeaways: meaning comes from human interpretation; correlation is not causation; and always check uncertainty, method, and motive behind a statistic.

Why this matters for ethics in computing: systems built on data can mislead or harm if the data is misread. Critical interpretation is an ethical duty for anyone who collects or presents information.

**⚠️ Student action required:** Watch all three TED Talks listed above and capture your reflections in your Reflection Log.

## Unit 5 — Empowerment Through Data and Data Use

### R09 — Empowerment Through Computing

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (9 of 24) · **Section:** 5.1 Empowerment Through Data · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Select an applied-computing article from IEEE, The Conversation, or Communications of the ACM (last two years) describing computing applied to solve a problem.
In a new thread in your Reflection Log, state:
- what problem is being solved by the computing used.
- whether solving it this way adds value to individuals or society (explain your opinion).
- which criteria you are using to make your assessment.

#### My Reflection

The applied-computing example I chose is the use of deep learning to screen for diabetic retinopathy, a leading cause of preventable blindness. A clinical validation study tested an AI system on retinal photographs in an under-resourced setting in Africa and found it could detect vision-threatening retinopathy with accuracy close to that of human specialists (Bellemo et al., 2019).

**What problem is being solved?** Diabetes is rising fastest in low- and middle-income countries, and there are not nearly enough eye specialists to screen everyone. Many people only discover the disease once their sight is already lost. The computing here lets a camera and an algorithm flag patients who need to see a specialist, so scarce expert time goes to those who truly need it.

**Does it add value?** In my opinion, yes, clearly. It reaches people who would otherwise get no screening at all and catches a condition that is treatable if found early. That is real empowerment, because it gives patients information and a chance to act before harm is permanent.

**Criteria I used:** I judged it on (1) whether it expands access to people previously left out, (2) whether the outcome is genuinely beneficial and not just convenient, (3) accuracy and safety, since a false negative could cost someone their sight, and (4) whether it supports rather than replaces human judgment. The study reports high sensitivity and keeps a specialist in the loop, so it meets my criteria. My one caution is that accuracy must be checked on the local population, not just assumed from the original training data.

### A08 — Coded Bias Film & Privacy TED Review

- **Type:** Action (8 of 20) · **Section:** 6.2–6.3 · **Status:** Done

#### Summary & Notes

This action pairs a TED Talk on privacy with a documentary on algorithmic bias. Finn Lützow-Holm Myrstad, of the Norwegian Consumer Council, explains "How tech companies deceive you into giving up your data and privacy." His team read the terms and conditions of the apps on an average phone, and it took nearly a day and a half. He shows how confusing legal language and "dark patterns" trick users into surrendering personal data at a scale they never imagined. The film "Coded Bias" (2020, directed by Shalini Kantayya) follows MIT researcher Joy Buolamwini, who discovered that facial-recognition systems failed to detect her dark-skinned face until she wore a white mask. Her "Gender Shades" study found error rates as high as 34.7% for darker-skinned women versus under 1% for lighter-skinned men. The film argues that algorithms absorb society's race and gender biases, are often used to surveil people without consent, and operate with little legal oversight, putting civil rights at risk.

Key takeaways: privacy is eroded through fine print and dark patterns, and AI systems can carry hidden, harmful bias that affects jobs, housing, and justice.

Why this matters for ethics in computing: these works show that technical systems are never neutral. Designers must test for bias, demand transparency, and respect informed consent.

### R10 — Critical Evaluation of Ethical Hacking

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (10 of 24) · **Section:** 6.4 Opening the Door to Bad Actors · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Using the Unit 3 critical-thinking framework and a Unit 2 philosophical lens, critically discuss ethical hacking.
Title the post: "Critical Evaluation of Ethical Hacking from a <philosophical lens> Perspective."
Include:
- a description paragraph answering what, when, who, and where.
- an analysis paragraph answering why and how.
- an evaluation paragraph answering what if, so what, and what does this mean.

*Required reading: Quinn, Ch. 7 'Computer and Network Security'.*

#### My Reflection

**Critical Evaluation of Ethical Hacking from a Utilitarian Perspective**

**Description (what, when, who, where).** Ethical hacking, also called penetration testing, is when authorized security professionals deliberately attack a computer system to find weaknesses before criminals do (Quinn, 2020). It happens today across almost every industry, from banks to hospitals to governments, and is carried out by hired testers, in-house security teams, and "red teams." It takes place wherever organizations run systems that hold valuable or sensitive data, increasingly including cloud services and connected devices.

**Analysis (why and how).** It exists because defending a system is harder than attacking it; defenders must close every hole, while an attacker needs only one. By thinking like an attacker, ethical hackers reveal the real holes rather than the ones a checklist assumes. How is it done? Through permission-based scanning, exploiting test weaknesses, social-engineering trials, and reporting findings so they can be fixed. The key feature that separates it from crime is consent: the owner agrees in advance to the testing and its scope.

**Evaluation (what if, so what, what does this mean).** What if ethical hacking did not exist? Vulnerabilities would mostly be found by criminals first, and far more people would be harmed by breaches. From a utilitarian lens, which judges actions by their overall outcomes, ethical hacking produces a large net good: a small, controlled, consented harm prevents much larger uncontrolled harm. So what? It means the same skill is ethical or unethical depending mainly on consent and intent, not on the technique itself. What this means for me is that I should support authorized testing in my own work and never treat "I was just testing" as an excuse for acting without permission.

**References**

Quinn, M. J. (2020). *Ethics for the information age* (8th ed.). Pearson.

### R11 — Right to Repair AI Systems

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (11 of 24) · **Section:** 6.5 Accidental Misuse · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Watch Rumman Chowdhury's TED Talk about your right to repair AI systems.
Post a reflection identifying typical causes that prevent owners of technologies from using them; in your opinion, who is responsible for resolving them?
In the same post, explain whether individuals need a right to repair technologies they own. Consider:
- Were the actions taken by farmers to gain control of their trackers ethical?
- Were the actions taken by John Deere ethical?

*Action after this: Complete and submit Assignment 2.*

#### My Reflection

Rumman Chowdhury's talk made me see how often we own a device but are not allowed to actually control it. The typical causes she points to are legal and technical locks: patents and licensing terms that make repair "illegal," software that only the manufacturer's technicians can unlock, and closed systems that hide how the AI works so owners cannot inspect or retrain it (Chowdhury, 2024). She uses the example of John Deere's smart tractors, where farmers were blocked from fixing their own equipment and had to wait weeks for an authorized technician while crops rotted.

In my opinion, responsibility for resolving this is shared but starts with the manufacturers, because they designed the locks. Regulators also have a role in setting right-to-repair rules, and Chowdhury argues users themselves should be allowed in to report issues and patch problems.

Do individuals need a right to repair what they own? I think yes. If you have bought something and it fails, being trapped while it sits broken is unfair, and for AI systems it is also a safety issue, since the people closest to the problem often understand it best.

*Were the farmers' actions ethical?* Mostly yes. Working with hackers to regain use of equipment they legally owned was a reasonable response to being locked out, and the harm they prevented (lost crops) was real. The grey area is that some methods skirted the law, so it was civil disobedience rather than clearly clean conduct.

*Were John Deere's actions ethical?* I think largely not. Using patents to monopolize repair protected company revenue at the direct expense of the owners' livelihoods, which fails both a rights test and a fairness test. Some lock-down can be defended for safety, but blocking all repair goes too far.

**References**

Chowdhury, R. (2024, June). *Your right to repair AI systems* [Video]. TED. https://www.ted.com/talks/rumman_chowdhury_your_right_to_repair_ai_systems

## Unit 7 — Algorithms, Models, and Their Uses

### A10 — Alignment & Frame Problem Videos

- **Type:** Action (10 of 20) · **Section:** 7.2 Getting from Data to a Successful Outcome · **Status:** Done

#### Task

Watch Jonny Thomson's video explaining the alignment problem.
Watch Jonny Thomson's video explaining the frame problem and Daniel Dennett's thought experiment.

*Required reading: Marco Argenti, 'Why Engineers Should Study Philosophy' (HBR).*

#### Summary & Notes

This action explains two classic problems in AI through short videos and a required reading. The alignment problem asks how we make an AI actually pursue what we want, not just what we literally tell it. A system that optimizes the wrong goal can produce harmful side effects even while "succeeding," so aligning machine objectives with human values is hard and central to AI safety. The frame problem, illustrated by Daniel Dennett's famous robot-and-bomb thought experiment, is about knowing which facts are relevant after an action. In Dennett's story, the first robot pulls a wagon to save its battery but the bomb is on the same wagon; the next robot tries to consider every side effect and freezes, unable to decide what matters. The lesson is that humans effortlessly ignore irrelevant possibilities, but programming that common sense into a machine is extremely difficult. The required HBR reading, Marco Argenti's "Why Engineers Should Study Philosophy," argues that, as AI writes more code, the valuable human skill is asking the right "why" questions; philosophy trains critical thinking, ethics, and clear reasoning.

Key takeaways: getting an AI to do the right thing (alignment) and to know what is relevant (frame problem) are deep, unsolved challenges, and philosophical thinking helps engineers tackle them.

Why this matters for ethics in computing: these problems show why careful goal-setting and human judgment must guide powerful automated systems.

**⚠️ Student action required:** Watch Jonny Thomson's alignment and frame-problem videos and read Argenti's HBR article, then record reflections in your Reflection Log.

**References**

Thomson, J. (n.d.). *The alignment problem* [Video]. Big Think. https://bigthink.com/people/jonnythomson/

Dennett, D. C. (1984). Cognitive wheels: The frame problem of AI. In C. Hookway (Ed.), *Minds, machines and evolution* (pp. 129–151). Cambridge University Press.

Argenti, M. (2024, April 8). Why engineers should study philosophy. *Harvard Business Review*. https://hbr.org/2024/04/why-engineers-should-study-philosophy

### R12 — Issues Exacerbated by AI-Augmented Environments

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (12 of 24) · **Section:** 7.4 Use the Right Model for the Right Job · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Post a reflection: What other known issues in software engineering or data science can be exacerbated by an AI-augmented environment?
There are no wrong answers — extend your curiosity about your discipline.

#### My Reflection

Thinking about my own discipline, I realized that AI does not usually create brand-new problems; it takes problems software engineering and data science already had and makes them bigger and faster.

The first one that comes to mind is **technical debt**. We already cut corners under deadline pressure, but when an AI tool generates a lot of code quickly, it is easy to accept code nobody fully understands. The debt piles up faster than before, and it is harder to spot. A related issue is **over-trust in automation**. We have long known about "automation bias," where people stop double-checking a system because it is usually right. An AI assistant that sounds confident makes this worse, and I can imagine accepting a wrong suggestion just because it was phrased well.

A second area is **data quality and bias**. Garbage-in, garbage-out has always been true, but AI scales it. If the training data is skewed, the model spreads that skew across thousands of decisions, and the bias hides behind a layer of math that looks objective. **Reproducibility** also suffers, because large models can behave differently on the same input, making bugs hard to trace.

Finally, **accountability and skill erosion** worry me. When work is split between a person and an AI, it gets murky who is responsible when something fails. And if junior developers lean on AI for the basics, they may never build the deeper understanding needed to catch its mistakes.

So my take is that an AI-augmented environment is a kind of amplifier: it speeds up good practices and bad ones alike, which means our discipline needs stronger review habits, not weaker ones.

---

### R13 — Algorithmic Reach (O'Neil + TED Talk)

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (13 of 24) · **Section:** 7.5 Algorithmic Reach · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Watch one TED Talk about algorithms (from the provided list or your own search).
Post a reflection considering if/how the ethical questions raised by Cathy O'Neil relate to the talk you chose.
- Does the algorithm you are considering do more than its intended outcome?
- What are the risks of an algorithm reaching past its intended use?

#### My Reflection

The TED talk I chose is Kevin Slavin's "How algorithms shape our world" (Slavin, 2011). His main point is that algorithms, especially in finance, have grown so powerful and fast that they now shape the physical and economic world in ways no single person designed or fully understands. He uses examples like high-frequency trading algorithms that caused the 2010 "flash crash" and companies hollowing out buildings just to place servers closer to an exchange.

This connects closely to Cathy O'Neil's questions. O'Neil argues that harmful models, what she calls "weapons of math destruction," are often opaque, large-scale, and damaging, and that we treat their output as objective truth even when it is not (O'Neil, 2016). Slavin's talk is the same worry from a different angle: he shows algorithms acting beyond anyone's intention or control, while O'Neil shows the human cost when that happens.

**Does the algorithm do more than its intended outcome?** Yes. Trading algorithms were meant to buy and sell efficiently, but together they reshaped markets, triggered crashes, and even changed real estate decisions. That is far past the original goal.

**What are the risks of an algorithm reaching past its intended use?** The big ones are loss of control, because behaviour emerges that no one planned; lack of accountability, because it is unclear who answers for an automated outcome; and unfair harm to people who never agreed to be subject to the system. Both speakers push me to the same conclusion: we should keep humans able to understand and override these systems before their reach exceeds our oversight.

**References**

O'Neil, C. (2016). *Weapons of math destruction: How big data increases inequality and threatens democracy*. Crown.

Slavin, K. (2011, July). *How algorithms shape our world* [Video]. TED. https://www.ted.com/talks/kevin_slavin_how_algorithms_shape_our_world

This action asks you to pick one TED Talk about algorithms and watch it (or find another on the same theme). A strong, widely used choice is Kevin Slavin's "How algorithms shape our world." Slavin argues that we increasingly live in a world designed for and controlled by algorithms we no longer fully understand. He describes how automated programs set stock prices, choose which movies get made, drive Netflix and Amazon recommendations, and even influence physical architecture (buildings hollowed out for trading servers). His most striking example is the Wall Street "Flash Crash" of May 6, 2010, when about 9% of the U.S. stock market vanished in roughly five minutes because of interacting trading algorithms. His warning: we are writing code that is "no longer legible," with effects we cannot fully predict or control. Other talks on the unit list make similar points about recommendation systems, ranking, and automated decision-making. Choose whichever talk best fits your interests for Reflection R13.

Key takeaways: algorithms have shifted from describing the world to actively shaping it, and their growing complexity makes them hard to understand or oversee.

Why this matters for ethics in computing: when no single person understands a system's behavior, accountability becomes difficult. Designers must value transparency, testing, and human oversight.

**⚠️ Student action required:** Choose and watch one TED Talk about algorithms, then record your reflections in Reflection R13 (Algorithmic Reach).

**References**

Slavin, K. (2011, July). *How algorithms shape our world* [Video]. TED. https://www.ted.com/talks/kevin_slavin_how_algorithms_shape_our_world

### R14 — Washington DC Teachers' Algorithm

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (14 of 24) · **Section:** 7.6 Algorithmic Impacts · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Post a reflection on the ethical questions O'Neil raises about the Washington, DC teacher evaluation algorithm:
- Who is impacted other than the teacher? What is the true reach?
- What ethical issues might arise in creating/using the algorithm? Could there have been warning signs?
- Who is responsible for the output? Explain the different responsibilities of different parties.
Then find another news story where an algorithm's reach went farther than intended and explain your choice.

*Required reading: Joanna Redden (2018); O'Neil, intro to Weapons of Math Destruction (2016).*

#### My Reflection

O'Neil tells the story of Sarah Wysocki, a fifth-grade teacher in Washington, DC who was fired after the IMPACT value-added model gave her a low score, even though her principal, colleagues, and parents rated her highly. She could not even learn how the score was calculated because the model was proprietary (O'Neil, 2016).

**Who else is impacted? What is the true reach?** Far more than the teacher. Her students lose a teacher they liked, the parents lose trust in the school, and the other 205 teachers fired alongside her are affected too. The reach also spreads sideways: remaining teachers may start "teaching to the test" or even cheat to protect their scores, which O'Neil notes actually happened, and that harms future students. So one model reshaped the behaviour of an entire school system.

**What ethical issues arise, and were there warning signs?** The main issues are opacity (no one could see or challenge the formula), poor validity (judging a teacher on a small, noisy sample of test scores), and unfairness (a "feedback loop" where bad inputs produce bad firings). The warning signs were clear: the score flatly contradicted every human review, and the sample size was tiny. A contradiction that large should have triggered a second look.

**Who is responsible?** Responsibility is shared. The district that chose to fire people based on one number holds the most, because it acted on output it did not understand. The vendor (Mathematica) is responsible for building a model that could not be explained or audited. Policymakers who demanded a quick "objective" metric share blame for the pressure. The model itself is not a moral agent; the humans who built and used it are.

**Another story — the Dutch childcare benefits scandal.** The Netherlands used a risk-scoring algorithm to detect childcare-benefit fraud. It wrongly flagged tens of thousands of families, often from minority or dual-nationality backgrounds, forcing them to repay huge sums and pushing many into financial ruin; the scandal contributed to the government's resignation in 2021 (Heikkilä, 2022). I chose it because, like the teacher case, an algorithm meant to find a few bad actors reached far past its intended use and inflicted serious, hard-to-reverse harm on innocent people.

**References**

Heikkilä, M. (2022, March 29). *Dutch scandal serves as a warning for Europe over risks of using algorithms*. POLITICO. https://www.politico.eu/article/dutch-scandal-serves-as-a-warning-for-europe-over-risks-of-using-algorithms/

O'Neil, C. (2016). *Weapons of math destruction: How big data increases inequality and threatens democracy*. Crown.

## Unit 8 — Ethical Challenges in Modelling and Algorithms

### R15 — AI4People Five Guiding Principles

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (15 of 24) · **Section:** 8.1 Algorithmic Unintended Consequences · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Post a reflection: Identify and write a sentence, in your own words, describing each of the five guiding principles derived from the AI4People article.

*Required reading: AI4People Scientific Committee (2018) analysis of ethical principles for AI in society.*

#### My Reflection

The AI4People framework sets out five guiding principles for a "good AI society" (Floridi et al., 2018). The first four are borrowed from medical ethics, and the fifth is added specifically for AI. Here is each one in my own words:

1. **Beneficence — do good.** AI should be built to actually benefit people and the planet, promoting well-being and the common good rather than just being clever or profitable.

2. **Non-maleficence — do no harm.** Even when AI is meant to help, we must prevent it from causing harm, whether through misuse, accidents, invasions of privacy, or unintended side effects.

3. **Autonomy — preserve human choice.** People should keep the power to decide; we delegate some decisions to machines, but humans must be able to take that power back and stay in control.

4. **Justice — be fair.** AI should share its benefits widely, avoid creating or deepening discrimination, and not concentrate advantage in the hands of a few.

5. **Explicability — be understandable and accountable.** Because the other four cannot be checked if AI is a black box, we must be able to understand how a system reaches its decisions (intelligibility) and know who is answerable for them (accountability).

What I find clever is that explicability is the glue: without being able to explain a system, we cannot judge whether it is doing good, avoiding harm, respecting autonomy, or being fair. That made the whole framework click for me.

**References**

Floridi, L., Cowls, J., Beltrametti, M., Chatila, R., Chazerand, P., Dignum, V., Luetge, C., Madelin, R., Pagallo, U., Rossi, F., Schafer, B., Valcke, P., & Vayena, E. (2018). AI4People—An ethical framework for a good AI society: Opportunities, risks, principles, and recommendations. *Minds and Machines, 28*(4), 689–707. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11023-018-9482-5

### A12 — Stuart Russell: Rewards & Risks of AI

- **Type:** Action (12 of 20) · **Section:** 8.1 Algorithmic Unintended Consequences · **Status:** Done

#### Task

Watch Stuart Russell's video about the long- and short-term rewards and risks of AI.

*Required readings in 8.1: Data Harm Record (Cardiff); Greenemeier on self-driving fatalities; students on generative AI in higher ed; AI4People principles.*

#### Summary & Notes

This action has you watch Stuart Russell, a leading AI researcher, discuss the short- and long-term rewards and risks of artificial intelligence. Russell starts from a clash of intuitions: Alan Turing warned about building machines smarter than us, yet many developers assume that would simply be good. The core danger is the value alignment problem, there is no guarantee a superintelligent system's goals would match human values. Russell lists near-term risks such as automated surveillance and persuasion, autonomous weapons, and economic disruption, alongside the long-term risk of losing control of systems more capable than ourselves. His proposed solution is "provably beneficial AI," built on principles that keep machines uncertain about human preferences and willing to defer to and learn from people, so they remain correctable rather than single-mindedly pursuing a fixed goal. Until such systems exist, he argues, regulation and a strong safety culture are needed. The unit pairs this with readings on real harms: Cardiff's Data Harm Record, reporting on self-driving fatalities, concerns about generative AI in higher education, and the AI4People ethical principles.

Key takeaways: AI offers large benefits but carries serious risks; safety must be designed in, with machines that defer to human values.

Why this matters for ethics in computing: it frames the central professional duty of keeping powerful systems controllable, transparent, and aligned with human interests.

**⚠️ Student action required:** Watch Stuart Russell's video and review the Section 8.1 readings (Data Harm Record, Greenemeier, generative-AI-in-education piece, AI4People), then record reflections in your Reflection Log.

### R16 — Ethical Issues vs. Controls Table

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (16 of 24) · **Section:** 8.2 Setting Boundaries · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Copy the table below and add a reflection at each intersection on whether/how each issue is met by each action.
- Which intersections do you consider future challenges for AI ethics? Why?
- Describe any other ethical issues you notice that are not captured on the table.

*Required reading: CBC article in which Redden calls for more public debate and transparency around AI use.*

#### My Reflection

Here is the table with a short note at each intersection on how (or whether) the control action meets each ethical issue.

| | Transparency Requirements | Privacy Protection | Safety Protocols & Bias Mitigation | Accountability Mechanisms | Societal Impact |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Deployment Restrictions and Human Rights** | Met partly: rules on where AI may be used can require public disclosure of restricted uses. | Met well: banning high-risk uses (e.g., mass surveillance) directly protects privacy. | Met partly: restrictions stop the most dangerous uses but do not fix bias inside allowed uses. | Met well: legal limits create clear lines someone can be held to. | Met strongly: this is mainly about protecting society from harmful deployment. |
| **Responsible Human Oversight** | Met partly: a human reviewer can explain a decision only if the system is already explainable. | Met indirectly: oversight can catch privacy misuse but is not a privacy control itself. | Met well: a human in the loop can stop unsafe or biased outputs before harm. | Met strongly: oversight names a responsible person, which is the core of accountability. | Met partly: depends on whether overseers act in the public interest. |
| **Transparency and Technical Safeguards** | Met strongly: this is the direct control for transparency (documentation, model cards, logs). | Met well: safeguards like encryption and data minimization protect privacy. | Met well: technical tests for bias and safety live here. | Met partly: logs support accountability but someone must still act on them. | Met partly: transparency builds public trust but does not guarantee good outcomes. |
| **Testing, Verification, and Evaluation** | Met partly: results must be reported openly to count as transparency. | Met partly: testing can reveal privacy leaks but is not aimed at privacy. | Met strongly: this is the main control for safety and bias detection. | Met well: documented testing shows due diligence if something goes wrong. | Met well: ongoing evaluation catches harmful societal effects over time. |

**Which intersections are future challenges? Why?** I think the hardest will be *Responsible Human Oversight × Transparency* and *Transparency × Societal Impact*. As models get more complex, "having a human in the loop" means little if that human cannot actually understand the system, and being technically transparent does not guarantee the public can meaningfully debate the impact. Redden makes a similar point, calling for far more public debate and openness about how governments use AI, not just technical fixes (CBC News, 2018).

**Other ethical issues not on the table.** A few are missing: environmental cost (the energy and water used to train large models), labour issues (the low-paid workers who label data and moderate content), consent for the data used to train models, and the long-term concentration of power in a handful of companies that own the biggest systems.

**References**

CBC News. (2018). *Researcher calls for more public debate and transparency around government use of AI*. CBC. https://www.cbc.ca/news/

### R17 — Digital Twins Pros and Cons

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (17 of 24) · **Section:** 8.3 Deliberate Misuse · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Watch the video about digital twins.
Post a reflection listing pros and cons of creating a digital twin for each learner in this course, based on ethical ideas and challenges.

#### My Reflection

A digital twin is a live virtual model of a real thing, fed by ongoing data so it mirrors and predicts the real version's behaviour (IBM, n.d.). Imagining a digital twin of each learner in this course, a model of how I study, what I struggle with, and how I am likely to perform, brought up clear pros and cons when I weighed it against the ethical ideas we have covered.

**Pros**
- *Beneficence:* it could personalize learning, spotting where I am about to fall behind and suggesting help before I fail, which genuinely supports my success.
- *Efficiency and fairness:* instructors could find learners who need extra support early, instead of only after a bad grade, which could help students who are usually overlooked.
- *Safety to experiment:* the twin could test "what if I changed my study plan?" without real consequences for my marks.

**Cons**
- *Privacy:* a twin needs deep, continuous data about my behaviour, which is highly sensitive and could be misused, breached, or sold.
- *Autonomy:* if the model predicts I will fail, that label could follow me and shape how instructors treat me, nudging me down a path I did not choose. This is a feedback-loop risk like O'Neil warns about.
- *Bias and accuracy:* the twin is only as good as its data; if it learns from biased patterns, it could unfairly write off certain learners.
- *Consent and accountability:* who owns my twin, who can see it, and who is responsible if it is wrong? Those questions are not clearly answered.

My overall view is that a learner digital twin could be powerful and helpful, but only with strong consent, transparency, and the right to see and challenge my own twin. Without those, the privacy and autonomy costs outweigh the benefits.

**References**

IBM. (n.d.). *What is a digital twin?* https://www.ibm.com/topics/what-is-a-digital-twin

### R18 — Ethics of Generative AI Used in This Unit

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (18 of 24) · **Section:** 8.3 Deliberate Misuse · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Some of this unit was written with input from generative AI tools. Post a reflection:
- In your view, is this ethical? Explain why, referring to your own philosophical point of view.
- Give at least three considerations about the generative AI output your instructor needed to make before including it.

*Action after this: Complete and submit Assignment 3.*

#### My Reflection

In my view, using generative AI to help write part of this unit can be ethical, but only with conditions, and the most important one is honesty about it. My own point of view leans on a mix of duty and consequences. From a duty angle, I think there is an obligation to be truthful with students about how material was made, which is exactly what the instructor did by telling us. From a consequences angle, if the AI helped produce clearer, accurate material faster, and a human checked it, the outcome is good for learners. So the disclosure is what makes it sit right with me; quietly passing AI text off as fully human-written would feel deceptive and would fail the honesty duty.

Before including any generative AI output, I think the instructor needed to make at least these considerations:

1. **Accuracy.** Generative AI can produce confident but wrong information ("hallucinations"), so the instructor had to fact-check every claim against reliable sources before trusting it.

2. **Bias and fairness.** These tools learn from large web datasets that carry social biases, so the instructor needed to check the output did not present a skewed or one-sided view, which matters a lot in an ethics course.

3. **Copyright and originality.** Because models are trained on others' work, the instructor had to make sure the text was not unintentionally copying a source and that it respected intellectual property, modelling the academic integrity students are held to.

A fourth I would add is appropriateness for the audience, making sure the tone and level actually fit learners. Overall, I think transparency plus careful human review is what turns AI assistance from a shortcut into a defensible choice.

**References**

Floridi, L., Cowls, J., Beltrametti, M., Chatila, R., Chazerand, P., Dignum, V., Luetge, C., Madelin, R., Pagallo, U., Rossi, F., Schafer, B., Valcke, P., & Vayena, E. (2018). AI4People—An ethical framework for a good AI society. *Minds and Machines, 28*(4), 689–707. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11023-018-9482-5

### R19 — Releasing Known-Flawed Innovative Technology

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (19 of 24) · **Section:** 9.5 Accountability · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Post a reflection: Is it ethically acceptable to develop and release an innovative technology known to include errors, use illegal data sources, and have negative environmental or social impacts?
Is taking an unsustainable approach to development ethical in the short term for long-term gain?

*Related action: Listen to CIPO's Canadian IP Voices Podcast Ep. 26 on AI-generated creations.*

#### My Reflection

My honest answer is no, releasing technology that you already know contains errors, relies on illegal data, and causes environmental or social harm is not ethically acceptable. I want to be careful, though, because "errors" needs unpacking. All software ships with some bugs, and waiting for perfection would mean releasing nothing. So the real question is about *known, serious* flaws plus illegal data plus known harm, taken together.

Looking at it through more than one lens helps. From a duty/rights view, using illegal data sources violates other people's rights from the start, so the project is built on a wrong no matter how useful the result is. From a consequences view, knowingly causing environmental or social damage means you are trading other people's well-being for your gain, and the harm is real while the benefit is only hoped for. Both lenses point the same way. Accountability also matters: if you know in advance and release anyway, you cannot later claim it was an accident.

Is an unsustainable, "move fast and clean up later" approach ethical for long-term gain? I am skeptical. It assumes the long-term gain will actually arrive and will outweigh the damage, but that is a guess, and the harm is certain and often falls on people who never agreed to it. History shows the "later" cleanup frequently never happens. The current debate over AI-generated creations and who owns or is liable for them, raised in CIPO's IP Voices podcast, is a good example of harms and rights questions arriving faster than the rules to handle them (Canadian Intellectual Property Office, 2021). My position: fix the illegal-data and known-harm problems first, then release, even if it is slower.

**References**

Canadian Intellectual Property Office. (n.d.). *Canadian IP Voices* [Audio podcast], Episode 26: AI-generated creations. Government of Canada. https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/canadian-intellectual-property-office/en/canadian-ip-voices

### A16 — CIPO IP Podcast: AI-Generated Creations

- **Type:** Action (16 of 20) · **Section:** 9.5 Accountability · **Status:** Done
- *Supports Reflection R19 (Releasing Known-Flawed Technology).*

#### Task

Listen to CIPO's Canadian IP Voices Podcast, Episode 26: 'Who owns AI-Generated Creations (and Why You Should Care)'.

#### Summary & Notes

This action has you listen to Episode 26 of the Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO) "Canadian IP Voices" podcast, titled "Who owns AI-generated creations (and why you should care)." The guest, IP litigator Guillaume Lavoie Ste-Marie of Smart & Biggar, explains how copyright law applies (or fails to apply) to works made with tools like ChatGPT. A key point is that, under Canadian law, copyright requires originality, meaning a human author must exercise skill and judgment, and the language of the Copyright Act strongly suggests the author must be a human being. That raises a hard question: if an AI produces text, images, or music, who, if anyone, owns it? Because most countries follow the Berne Convention, which grants automatic copyright to human-made original works, nations are now being forced to decide how to treat purely AI-generated output. The guest advises users to read the license terms of any AI tool before creating works with it, and to be careful about feeding original or confidential information into AI systems.

Key takeaways: current copyright law centers on human authorship, AI-generated works sit in a legal gray zone, and users should understand tool licenses and protect confidential inputs.

Why this matters for ethics in computing: ownership, credit, and accountability for AI output are growing ethical and legal issues that affect creators, companies, and the public.

**⚠️ Student action required:** Listen to CIPO Canadian IP Voices Episode 26 and record reflections supporting Reflection R19 (Releasing Known-Flawed Technology).

### R20 — Information Availability as a Defining Factor of Society

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (20 of 24) · **Section:** 9.6 Societal Impact · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Post a reflection: Using what you know about logical thinking, do you consider the information available to people in a society to be a major defining factor of that society?
Present a short, logical argument for your position.

*Required reading: NIST article on bias in AI; NIST Sec. 3 on AI bias challenges/guidance; reading on cognitive bias in XAI.*

#### My Reflection

Yes, I do think the information available to people is a major defining factor of a society. Let me lay it out as a short logical argument.

Premise 1: People make their decisions based on the information they can access. We cannot act on what we do not know.

Premise 2: The decisions people make, about how to vote, what to buy, who to trust, and what is true, shape a society's institutions, economy, and culture.

Premise 3: Today, much of the information people receive is filtered and ranked by algorithms, and those algorithms can carry bias from their training data, which shapes what people see and believe (Schwartz et al., 2022).

Conclusion: Therefore, what information is available, and how it is filtered, strongly shapes the decisions people make, and through them the kind of society that results. So information availability is a major defining factor.

I want to be careful not to overstate it. Information is not the *only* factor; geography, history, resources, and power also shape societies, so I would call it "a major defining factor," not "the" single cause. But the logical chain above holds even after that qualification. What strengthened the argument for me was the NIST work on AI bias, which points out that bias is not just a technical glitch in the data but also comes from human and systemic sources, so the very systems that decide what information reaches us can quietly skew a society's shared picture of reality (Schwartz et al., 2022). That makes information availability not just important, but something we have an ethical duty to keep fair and open.

**References**

Schwartz, R., Vassilev, A., Greene, K., Perine, L., Burt, A., & Hall, P. (2022). *Towards a standard for identifying and managing bias in artificial intelligence* (NIST Special Publication 1270). National Institute of Standards and Technology. https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.1270

### R21 — Microsoft Generative AI Business Case

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (21 of 24) · **Section:** 9.6 Societal Impact · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Review Microsoft's blog examples of customers using generative AI; select one business case and summarize the use case in your log.
Using common ethical areas of concern, identify and note any issues that might arise from the use described.

#### My Reflection

**The business case I chose:** Dentsu, a global marketing company, featured in Microsoft's customer stories. Dentsu built a "copilot" using Azure OpenAI Service and Azure Machine Learning so employees could ask questions in plain language and have the tool interpret advertising-campaign results for them. Microsoft reports this cut analysis time by about 80% and promised millions in savings (Microsoft, 2024).

**Summary of the use case:** Instead of analysts manually digging through campaign data, staff chat with an AI assistant that summarizes results and explains what the numbers mean. The goal is faster insight and freeing skilled people from repetitive analysis.

**Ethical issues that might arise**, using common areas of concern:

- *Accuracy and reliability:* generative AI can produce confident but wrong summaries. If a marketing decision worth millions rests on a hallucinated insight, the business and its clients could be misled.
- *Transparency:* if staff cannot see how the assistant reached a conclusion, they may trust it without understanding it, an automation-bias risk.
- *Privacy and data security:* campaign data may include personal or client-confidential information. Sending it through an AI service raises questions about where the data goes and who can access it.
- *Job impact:* an 80% cut in analysis time is good for the company but may reduce the need for junior analysts, which is a real social concern.
- *Accountability:* if the AI's summary leads to a bad campaign, who is responsible, the employee, Dentsu, or Microsoft? That line is not obvious.

My takeaway is that the productivity gains are genuine, but they only stay ethical if a human keeps verifying the output, the data is handled securely, and someone clearly owns the results.

**References**

### A17 — Global Story Podcast: AI & Elections

- **Type:** Action (17 of 20) · **Section:** 9.6 Societal Impact · **Status:** Done

#### Task

Listen to The Global Story podcast where two leading experts discuss AI and democracy/elections.

#### Summary & Notes

This action has you listen to a BBC "The Global Story" podcast episode, "How artificial intelligence could upend 2024's many elections," where leading experts discuss AI's effect on democracy. The episode focuses on deepfakes, distrust, and democracy in a year when many of the world's most populous countries, including India and the United States (the Biden/Trump race), held elections. The experts, who have delivered the prestigious BBC Reith Lectures, warn that AI makes it cheap and easy to create convincing fake images, audio, and video, and to target voters with personalized persuasion. OpenAI's Sam Altman is quoted warning of "a new kind of interference that was just not possible before AI." The discussion weighs how synthetic media could spread misinformation, erode trust in real evidence, and undermine fair elections, while also noting possible safeguards such as content labeling, platform policies, and public awareness.

Key takeaways: AI-generated content threatens election integrity by making misinformation easier to produce and harder to detect, and by enabling micro-targeted manipulation; protecting democracy will require technical, legal, and educational responses.

Why this matters for ethics in computing: tools that generate or spread information carry direct consequences for democratic societies, making honesty, transparency, and abuse-prevention central ethical concerns for technologists.

### R22 — Role Responsibility & Desired Supports

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (22 of 24) · **Section:** 9.7 Trust in Computer-Based Systems · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Post a reflection:
- Consider your responsibility as a user, data scientist, coder, or software engineer in using/developing a system. Clearly state the role perspective; detail when you might be legally liable and when morally responsible.
- Consider what supports (legal, professional, organizational, or technical) you would like in place to help you maintain an ethical position in your role.

*Required reading: Coveney & Highfield on trusting computers.*

#### My Reflection

I will write from the perspective of a **software engineer/developer**, since that is closest to my work.

**When am I legally liable, and when morally responsible?** These are not the same thing, and separating them helped me. I am *legally liable* when I break a law or contract, for example if I knowingly ship code that mishandles personal data against privacy law like PIPEDA, ignore a safety standard, or violate the terms I signed with an employer or client. Legal liability is usually about clear duties and provable breaches. I am *morally responsible* in a wider set of cases, including ones where no law was broken. If I notice a feature could harm users and say nothing, or I cut a corner I know is risky because no one is watching, I am morally responsible even if I never get sued. Coveney and Highfield's point that we tend to over-trust computers is useful here: because users assume the system is right, the developer who built it carries a moral weight to make sure that trust is deserved (Coveney & Highfield, as cited in COMP351 Unit 9 readings). So my rule of thumb is that legal liability is the floor, and moral responsibility goes well above it.

**What supports would I want to maintain an ethical position?** I grouped them:
- *Legal/professional:* clear laws and a professional code of ethics (like ACM's) that I can point to when I push back, plus whistleblower protection so raising a concern does not cost me my job.
- *Organizational:* a culture where it is safe to say "this is not ready," realistic deadlines, and a named person responsible for ethics review, so it is not all on the individual.
- *Technical:* good testing tools, bias and security checks built into our pipeline, logging and documentation so decisions can be traced, and human-in-the-loop checkpoints for high-impact features.

With those supports, doing the right thing becomes the normal path rather than an act of courage.

**References**

Coveney, P., & Highfield, R. (n.d.). *On trusting computers* [Required reading, COMP351 Unit 9]. Athabasca University. (Full publication details as provided in the course materials.)

## Unit 10 — Future Development and Perspectives

### R23 — Harari & Li: Ongoing AI Concerns

- **Type:** 🧭 Reflection (23 of 24) · **Section:** 10.0 Introduction and Outcomes · **Status:** Posted

#### Task

Watch the Buolamwini–Altman discussion and the Harari–Li discussion on AI's spread across society.
Post a reflection: From your point of view, which of the concerns from Harari and Li's discussion are still concerns now that generative AI is widely available and the European AI Act is law?

#### My Reflection

In the Harari–Li discussion, Harari's biggest worry was that AI combined with brain and behaviour data could lead to "hacking humans," meaning a system that understands us better than we understand ourselves and can therefore manipulate us, and that this threatens human agency and democracy. Li's concerns were more grounded in the present: machine-learning bias, lack of diversity in who builds AI, privacy, and job displacement, and she stressed that solving these needs many disciplines working together (Stanford HAI, 2019). Joy Buolamwini's work on facial-recognition bias adds the warning that these systems already fail people unequally, especially women and people with darker skin (Buolamwini & Gebru, 2018).

Looking at this now that generative AI is everywhere and the EU AI Act is law, I think almost all of these concerns are still live, and some have grown.

Harari's "manipulation" fear feels more real than ever. Recommendation and generative systems now shape what billions of people read, and AI can generate persuasive text and deepfakes at scale, which is exactly the agency-and-democracy risk he described. The EU AI Act tries to address parts of this by banning some manipulative uses and labelling AI content, but enforcement is just beginning, so the worry remains.

Li's concerns are also still here. Bias has not been "solved"; generative models still reflect the skew in their training data, which is what Buolamwini warned about. Privacy is arguably worse, because these models are trained on huge scrapes of personal data. Job displacement has moved from theory to active debate as generative tools enter offices.

If anything, the EU AI Act validates these speakers: a risk-based law exists precisely because the harms they named turned out to be real. So my view is that their concerns aged well, and the new tools have made them more urgent, not less.

**References**

Buolamwini, J., & Gebru, T. (2018). Gender shades: Intersectional accuracy disparities in commercial gender classification. *Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, 81*, 1–15. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v81/buolamwini18a.html

Stanford HAI. (2019, April 22). *The historian and the technologist: Yuval Harari and Fei-Fei Li in discussion*. Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI. https://hai.stanford.edu/news/historian-and-technologist-yuval-harari-and-fei-fei-li-discussion
